questions.prompt: Explain what a protocol is in Swift, how types conform to it, and how protocols differ from classes.

rubric.criterion: Explains that a protocol is a blueprint/contract of properties and methods without storage
Explains that classes, structs, and enumerations can conform to protocols by implementing requirements
Contrasts with classes, noting protocols enable horizontal composition across value and reference types

questions.modelAnswer: A protocol defines a blueprint of methods, properties, and requirements without providing storage or implementation. Structs, enums, and classes conform to a protocol by implementing its declared requirements. Unlike class inheritance, protocols allow both value types and reference types to share behaviors horizontally.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between { get } and { get set } in protocol property requirements?

rubric.criterion: Explains that { get } requires read access and can be satisfied by let, var, or read-only/read-write computed properties
Explains that { get set } requires read and write access, requiring a mutable var or read-write computed property

questions.modelAnswer: A { get } requirement only demands read access. It can be satisfied by a constant let, a stored var, or a read-only computed property. A { get set } requirement demands both read and write access, which must be satisfied by a mutable stored var or a read-write computed property.

questions.prompt: Why do delegate protocols inherit from AnyObject, and why must delegates be declared weak?

rubric.criterion: Explains that AnyObject restricts protocol conformance to classes (reference types)
Explains that weak references prevent retain cycles between objects and can only hold class instances

questions.modelAnswer: Delegate protocols inherit from AnyObject to restrict conformance to class instances. In the delegate pattern, the delegating object holds its delegate as a weak reference to prevent retain cycles. Because ARC can only manage weak references on reference types, the protocol must be class-only.

questions.prompt: Explain the purpose of the mutating keyword in protocol method declarations and how classes handle it.

rubric.criterion: Explains that mutating in protocols allows value types (structs and enums) to modify self inside the method
Explains that classes conform to mutating requirements without writing the mutating keyword

questions.modelAnswer: The mutating keyword in a protocol declaration indicates that conforming value types (structs and enums) are permitted to modify their stored properties or self. When classes conform to a mutating protocol method, they omit the mutating keyword because class methods mutate reference types without copying.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between existential types (any Protocol) and opaque types (some Protocol)?

rubric.criterion: Explains that any Protocol is an existential container with dynamic dispatch and boxing overhead
Explains that some Protocol is an opaque type with a single concrete type known to the compiler, enabling static dispatch

questions.modelAnswer: An existential type (any Protocol) creates a runtime container that can hold different conforming types dynamically, incurring boxing and protocol witness table dispatch costs. An opaque type (some Protocol) represents one specific concrete type known to the compiler, hiding its identity while enabling static dispatch and inlining.
